text: An agent fixing a bug in a large codebase may take a hundred steps, and every step adds tool output to its transcript. Eventually the transcript outgrows the context window. Long before that, two other problems appear: models use very long contexts less reliably, and the agent becomes expensive, because at every step the whole transcript is sent to the model again.

That cost grows faster than you might expect. If each step adds roughly the same amount of text, then the hundredth step rereads ninety nine steps of history, and the total over the whole task grows with the square of the number of steps. Prompt caching lowers the price of rereading an unchanged prefix, but it does nothing to make the window bigger, so the transcript itself has to be managed.

The main technique is compaction. When the transcript passes a threshold, the harness asks the model to summarise the older part of the conversation, then replaces those turns with the summary while keeping the instructions, the task and the most recent turns word for word. It works like a laboratory notebook: you do not reread every page before each experiment, you read the summary of what has been established so far.

A good summary keeps what the agent will need again, such as decisions taken, open questions, file names and the errors already seen, and it drops raw tool output that has already been digested. Because a summary loses detail permanently, careful harnesses write the full outputs to disk before compacting, so that the agent can fetch an exact detail later if the summary turns out to be too brief.

Memory can also live outside the context altogether. An agent can be given tools to write notes to a file and read them back, a scratchpad that survives compaction and even separate sessions. When the notes grow large, they can be embedded and searched, so the agent retrieves only the memories relevant to its current step, using exactly the retrieval methods from earlier in this module.

The last technique is delegation. A main agent can hand a self contained subtask, such as searching a codebase for every caller of a function, to a subagent that starts with a fresh, empty context. The subagent does the messy exploration and returns only a short result, the way a manager asks a colleague for a one page brief rather than taking delivery of the entire archive.

Compaction, external notes and subagents all trade completeness for focus, and each can fail quietly, by dropping a fact the agent later needed. That raises the question this module has been circling: when you change a prompt, a model or a memory policy, how do you know whether the system actually improved? The next lesson is about evaluation.
